solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Like nothing obscure

definitions.meaning: nothing is the figure zero, whose shape is an oval, so like it means oval-shaped
writing that leaves out words and is hard to follow is called this

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: an oval shape like a zero, and speech so compressed that its meaning is unclear.

clue.text: Award judge leaving force

indicators.note: leaving says the judge's letter departs from the word for force

parts.note: to jemmy a door is to force it open with a crowbar

explanation.surface: A judge quits the police force and is given an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like the police, but it is a verb: JEMMY, to prise open, loses J.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emmy is the American television industry's annual prize, a statuette given for excellence.

clue.text: City group caught out French designer

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles

indicators.note: out says the cricket letter for caught is removed from the group word

parts.note: a clique is an exclusive group of people
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A city's in-crowd has unmasked a French designer.
explanation.definitionFit: René Lalique was a French glassmaker and jeweller famous for Art Nouveau and Art Deco pieces.

clue.text: Rainy? Cape tour gets rearranged, just in case

indicators.note: gets rearranged says the letters of the rainy cape tour words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: If the weather looks wet, the tour of the Cape is reshuffled as a safeguard.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done just in case is a precaution, an advance step taken against possible trouble.

clue.text: During more certain times, ultimately, they provide cover

parts.note: in means during, as in 'in the night'
surer is the comparative of sure, certain

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word times

explanation.surface: In more confident times, at last, people offer protection.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurance companies sell policies, which is what being covered against a loss means.

clue.text: Finished no-good pollsters

indicators.note: no-good says the letter for good is dropped from the pollsters' name

parts.note: Gallup is a well-known opinion-polling organisation

explanation.surface: Useless opinion pollsters are washed up.
explanation.walkthrough: G is the usual abbreviation for good.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying it is all up with someone is an idiom for being done for, beyond hope.

clue.text: One revered having dropped a knife

indicators.note: having dropped says the a is lost from the god's name

parts.note: Shiva is a Hindu god, one revered by worshippers

explanation.surface: Someone venerated has let a knife fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiv is slang for a knife, especially a makeshift blade used as a weapon.

clue.text: Stop daughter entering gallery in exciting night out?

parts.note: ho is an old call to halt, as in 'whoa'

indicators.note: entering puts the daughter letter inside the gallery's name

parts.note: the Tate is the London art gallery
D is the abbreviation for daughter in family trees

explanation.surface: A father stops his daughter going into an art gallery on what should be a thrilling evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A romantic evening with someone desirable is an exciting outing; the question mark admits the looseness.

clue.text: Showing backbone, lay vicar raised fee

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so these two pieces turn round

parts.note: to lay money on something is to bet
Rev is short for Reverend, the vicar's title
a rate is a charge or fee

explanation.surface: A lay vicar has put up his fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay vicar' reads as a church office, but lay is the verb wager.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, a creature with a spinal column; figuratively, someone with courage, both meanings of having backbone.

clue.text: Around noon, runner loses top to Reliant Robin's inventor

indicators.note: around says the shortened runner wraps about the noon letter
loses says a letter is taken from the runner

parts.note: a miler is an athlete who races over a mile

indicators.note: top to means the first letter of the word Reliant

explanation.surface: At about midday, a racer loses the roof of his Reliant Robin, a three-wheeled car.
explanation.walkthrough: The Reliant Robin is a British three-wheeled car, so 'Reliant Robin' looks like one thing; split it, and Robin is Christopher Robin.
explanation.definitionFit: A. A. Milne created Christopher Robin, the boy in the Winnie-the-Pooh stories, named after his own son.

clue.text: In which trawler endlessly sat at sea?

definitions.text: In which trawler endlessly sat at sea?

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled
endlessly says the word trawler loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A trawler sat at sea for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean is made of brine, the medium a fishing boat floats in when out on the waves.

clue.text: You and I wear tight pants outside church — one wants to be slimmer

parts.note: you and I together are we

indicators.note: outside says the jumbled letters go around the church abbreviation
pants as a verb means gasps, but here it is slang for rubbish, signalling a jumble

explanation.surface: We wear tight trousers outside church, though one of us wants to lose weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers, which suits the surface, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dieter, especially a member of the slimming organisation of that name, is one hoping to become thinner.

clue.text: Somehow acquit pedlar going round university once, then again and again and again

definitions.text: once, then again and again and again

indicators.note: going round says the jumbled letters enclose the university letter
somehow says the letters of acquit pedlar are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: A pedlar travelling round a university is somehow cleared.
explanation.definitionFit: Done in four identical copies, so one original plus three repeats, as the definition counts out.

clue.text: Bronte regularly let cast kiss in confined space

indicators.note: regularly picks every other letter of Bronte, starting with the first
cast means thrown into a new shape, so the letters of let are rearranged

parts.note: to neck is to kiss amorously

explanation.surface: Brontë's characters are allowed to kiss in a cramped place.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow neck where flow is restricted, such as a congested stretch of road, is a confined space.

clue.text: Capsize visible vessel

parts.note: overt means open and visible
an urn is a vessel

explanation.surface: A vessel that can be seen turns over.
explanation.definitionFit: To capsize is to tip over, the same as turning a boat upside down.

clue.text: My poem on the radio, listener

indicators.note: on the radio says the poem's word is heard, not seen

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
the ear is the organ of hearing, a listener

explanation.surface: A broadcaster presents his own poem to an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive, but it is the exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of dismay or surprise, interchangeable as interjections.

clue.text: Plant loaned out gutless engineer

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters of loaned are rearranged
gutless means with the insides removed, leaving only the outer letters of engineer

explanation.surface: A cowardly engineer has lent out a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleander is a poisonous evergreen Mediterranean shrub with pink or white flowers.

clue.text: Left working and working — it won't stick

indicators.note: working means being worked on, so the letters of left are reshaped

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Someone left at work, and keeps working, but it does not stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Teflon is the trade name for the non-stick coating used on frying pans.

clue.text: Ideal for 11, such could make fathers hers

parts.note: taking the three-letter word for plump out of fathers leaves hers, which is what the entry, read literally as an instruction, describes

explanation.surface: Something like this could turn fathers into hers.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is the slimmer, who would want low-fat food.
explanation.definitionFit: Food with no fat suits someone dieting to lose weight, the answer at 11.

clue.text: Wildest line in Ziggy Stardust's 'Time'?

indicators.note: in says the line letter goes inside the singer's name

parts.note: Ziggy Stardust was David Bowie's stage persona, so this is Bowie's

explanation.surface: Asks which lyric in a Bowie song about time is the most extreme.
explanation.definitionFit: The most gusty weather is the windiest and roughest, so wildest fits as a synonym.

clue.text: See Welsh girl, delightful

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, a bishop's see
Siân is a Welsh girl's name

explanation.surface: Look at the charming Welsh girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Elysium was the paradise of Greek myth, so something like it is blissful.

clue.text: Run from tramp after more left hostel in a reckless manner

indicators.note: after says the shortened tramp follows the word for more

parts.note: extra means more

indicators.note: from says the run letter is taken away from the tramp word

parts.note: a vagrant is a tramp
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
the Y is short for a YMCA hostel

explanation.surface: Someone flees a tramp after more people leave a hostel recklessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Spending or acting without restraint, wastefully and wildly, is acting recklessly.

clue.text: Scotsman fails to start religious group

indicators.note: fails to start says the name loses its opening letter

parts.note: Hamish is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A Scot does not join a religious group.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amish are a traditionalist Christian sect in America known for shunning modern technology.

clue.text: Remain without a leader in enemy uprising?

indicators.note: without says the a is removed from the remain word

parts.note: to stay is to remain

indicators.note: leader in means the first letter of enemy

explanation.surface: Holding out leaderless during an enemy revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a revolt, but it is a literal swelling on the eyelid.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful inflamed swelling on the eyelid is something that rises up on the skin.

clue.text: Morning Star journalist covers mobile library

indicators.note: covers says the journalist letters surround the jumbled library

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the crossword's usual journalist

indicators.note: mobile means moving, so the letters of library move around

explanation.surface: A reporter for the Morning Star newspaper writes about a mobile library.
explanation.walkthrough: The Morning Star is a British left-wing daily, but here it is someone who stars in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gets up very early shines in the morning, a playful reading of the phrase.

clue.text: Gent nearly involved with this crime could be seething

indicators.note: could be says the letters of seething can be rearranged from those of the shortened gent with the answer
nearly says the word gent stops short of its last letter

explanation.surface: A gentleman almost caught up in this crime could be fuming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' stands for the answer: GEN plus it shuffle to SEETHING.
explanation.definitionFit: A heist is a robbery, typically an audacious one, so a crime.

clue.text: Board look back

indicators.note: back says the look word is read backwards

parts.note: to peek is to take a quick look

explanation.surface: Climb aboard and look behind you.
explanation.definitionFit: Keep means board and lodging, as in earning your keep.

clue.text: Hot men drinking rum? Quite the opposite, for the near future

indicators.note: drinking means one piece swallows another
quite the opposite reverses the roles, so the rum word takes in the hot men

parts.note: rum is old slang for strange
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Steamy men drinking rum? No, the reverse, for the time ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Without 'Quite the opposite', the hot men would hold the rum; it makes the rum word take them in.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-range forecast covers only a brief time ahead, the immediate future.
